\# Invalid Reversal Signatures — Two-Sided Consolidation

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[Valid Reversal Signatures (The V-Shape)]]

## What it looks like

Price chops back and forth in a **two-sided consolidation** — lackluster closes, no clear directional commitment, just noise around a level. This is explicitly called out as something to never trust as a reversal signature, no matter how much it might visually resemble one.

## The companion invalid case: large wicks with no clear direction

The other version of an invalid setup is a candle (whether on the 4H or the 1H/30M) with an **extremely large wick** and very two-sided movement underneath it — the "reversal" is being formed entirely out of consolidation, with no clear directional commitment anywhere in the structure. When you see this — large wick on the higher timeframe *and* choppy, directionless movement on the lower timeframe underneath it — that's a fully invalid framework.

## What to do when you see this

**Skip it completely.** Don't try to salvage a trade out of a two-sided, lackluster structure. Wait instead for something like a fresh candle (a [[When C2 and C3 Both Fail to Manipulate (The C4 Case)|C3 or later]]) to open within a [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule|refined key level]] and give you an actual directional signature to trade away from.

\# Valid Reversal Signatures — The V-Shape

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]]

## What a valid signature looks like

Price **V-shapes away** from the level — a sharp, decisive move in one direction that reverses cleanly and closes strong, with no meaningful chop on the way. This strong-close V-shape is the signature you demand before trusting a reversal.

## Why this is a hard filter, not a preference

This is described as one of the biggest filters people struggle with. A lot of setups that *look* like reversals on the surface are actually just noisy consolidation that happened to end up moving in your direction — and those are not the same thing as a genuine reversal signature. Trusting the wrong one is one of the most common ways this framework gets misapplied.

## What to demand instead of accepting a weak signal

If price isn't giving you a clean V-shape, the correct response is to **demand expansion away** — specifically, a fair value gap forming as price finally commits to a direction. Once that gap forms, the entry is the **retracement into that gap**, not the initial messy move. See [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule]] for how this gap becomes your actual entry zone.

\# Intracandle Continuation — The Universal Model

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule]]

## When this applies

The current 4H candle **still has time left** and has **already expanded**, forming gaps on the hourly or 30-minute chart underneath it. You don't have to wait for the next 4H candle to open — you can trade the continuation *inside* the candle that's already moving.

## The method — same mechanic, applied mid-candle

1. Look for a **refined key level** (a gap, or what's referred to here as the "universal model") within the current 4H candle.
2. Price retraces into that gap.
3. A C2-style signature forms **within that gap** — a small, supportive wick showing the retracement is done.
4. Price expands away from it, toward the open draw.

## The one condition

This is only valid if there's still an **open draw** to trade toward. Without one, there's nothing to hold the trade toward — see [[The Two Non-Negotiables (Key Level and Open Draw)]].

\# The Fractal Alignment Filter — Daily, 4H, 1H

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]]

## The rule

Price is fractal, which means every profile has to **align across timeframes** before it's tradable. When trading, you want your **daily candle**, your **4H candle**, and your **1H candle** to all support expansion in the same direction you want price to go.

If any one of those timeframes doesn't support expansion in your intended direction, the setup fails this filter — regardless of how good the others look.

## Why this is a hard filter, not a bonus

This is the mechanism that keeps you from trading a 4H candle that *looks* like a valid reversal-to-expansion candle but is sitting inside a 1H candle that's actually still large-wicked and directionless. The 4H read alone is not enough — the smaller structure underneath it has to agree.

## How to apply it — top down

1. Start on the **daily** chart: does its wick support expansion in your direction? (Small wick = yes.)
2. Assuming you've traded into a key level, check the **4H**: is this a [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion|reversal-to-expansion candle]] (small wick) in your direction?
3. Drop to the **hourly**: does the candle you're actually trading *within* also support expansion? If the 4H looks valid but the hourly candle you're trading inside of has a large wick, **that hourly candle is your filter** — you do not trade it. Let it close and wait for the next one (C3) instead.

## What passing this filter looks like

Every layer — daily, 4H, hourly — shows a small wick supporting the same direction. When that alignment is present, you drop further to your entry timeframe (3-minute or 5-minute) and look for a strong V-shape reversal signature, positioning yourself in the lower quadrant of the aligned candle's width. See [[Example 1 - Top-Down Fractal Alignment Filter]] for the full worked version, including what it looks like when the hourly *fails* this check.

\# The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)]]

## The 50% open rule

A 4H candle that opens and **respects the previous 50% range of its C2 candle** is showing you something specific: it's opening inside the equilibrium of the prior move rather than chasing price into a fresh extreme. This is the first thing to check when fractalizing a 4H candle down to find your actual entry zone.

## The refined key level

Once that 50% respect is confirmed, **fractalize the candle further** to find a *refined* key level within it — typically an hourly PDA (a point of draw/interest) or an hourly gap, often sitting in a specific quadrant of the 4H candle's range (commonly the upper or lower quadrant, matching the direction you're trading).

The sequence:

1. Confirm the 4H candle opens respecting the previous 50%.
2. Find the refined key level inside it — usually a gap on the hourly chart.
3. Wait for price to **trade into that gap**.
4. Confirm a small, supportive wick forming there (the same [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion|small-wick logic]] applied at this lower-timeframe level).
5. Expand away from the gap toward the open draw.

## Why this exists

This is the practical answer to "where exactly do I get in." A 4H reversal thesis on its own doesn't give you a price to transact at — the refined key level is what turns the 4H idea into an actual, defined entry zone on a lower timeframe.

\# One-Stage Cracks for Continuations

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[Two-Stage Cracks for Reversals]]

## The rule

Unlike reversals, a **continuation** off a fair value gap only needs **one stage** of cracking correlation (SMT) — a single divergence, or "SMT fill," at the gap is sufficient to trade away from it.

## Why continuations need less confirmation than reversals

A continuation isn't claiming the market is about to reverse direction — it's claiming the market will keep doing what it's already doing. That's a smaller claim, structurally supported by the fact that a [[The Two Non-Negotiables (Key Level and Open Draw)|key level and open draw]] already exist. One divergence at the retracement gap is enough evidence to act on, where a reversal would need two.

## How this shows up in practice

Price retraces into a [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule|refined key level]] — a fair value gap — and a single SMT/crack forms right there. Combined with a small, supportive wick on that same candle, that's sufficient to position for the continuation toward the open draw. No second confirming candle is required the way it is for a reversal.

\# Two-Stage Cracks for Reversals

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]]

## The rule

A **reversal** off an ERL (external range liquidity) or key level requires **two stages of cracking correlation** (SMT) before it's tradable. One divergence is not enough for a reversal specifically — this is a stricter bar than continuations get (see [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]]).

## Stage 1 — at the key level (C1)

Price trades into the key level and forms its **first-stage crack**: the correlated asset does **not** take out the equivalent low/high that your asset is testing. This divergence at the level itself is the first stage.

## Stage 2 — at the C2 sweep

C2 opens, sweeps C1's low (or high), and forms a **second-stage crack** at that same low: again, the correlated asset does not take that low while your asset does. Two independent divergences — one at the original key level, one at the actual sweep — is what makes this a validated two-stage reversal.

## Why reversals need the extra confirmation

A reversal is a claim that the market is about to do the opposite of what it's been doing — that's a bigger claim than "this move will continue," so it demands more evidence. A single divergence could be coincidence; two independent divergences across two separate reactions to the same level is what earns the reversal enough conviction to trade.

## What comes after the two stages confirm

Once both stages are in place, check the candle's wick size (see [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion]]) — a small wick alongside the two-stage crack is what lets you expand directly from this candle. Then align the confirmation down through your fractal timeframes (hourly, then entry timeframe) — see [[Example 2 - Two-Stage SMT Reversal with 3-5 Minute Entry]] for the full worked case.

\# 0600 Reversal to 1000 Continuation

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Clock-time equivalent: [[0600 Reversal]] → [[1000 Reversal - Expansion]]

## The setup

06:00 reverses off a key level. You do **not** trade that reversal — you wait for it to confirm, then align the next 4H candle (10:00) as the continuation. Described as one of the highest-probability 4H profiles in the model **provided there is still an open draw**.

The confirmation logic runs backwards from the usual: you are not looking for a two-stage SMT to prove 06:00 reversed. The 10:00 continuation setting up correctly is itself the confirmation that 06:00 reversed.

## The key level inside the 06:00 candle

Three things count as the key level the continuation is framed from:

- a **gap**
- a **swing high or low**
- an **SMT**

An SMT specifically matters when price has disrespected a gap — if the gap gave way, you want divergence to have gone in before treating the reversal as real.

## Where the 10:00 wick has to form

The 10:00 wick must form **within the 50% (EQ) of the 06:00 candle**. That is what keeps the wick small enough to trade.

**Which 50% to measure:** normally the whole 06:00 candle. But if that candle *closed beyond its own equilibrium*, measure the **EQ of the wick instead** — the wick is what has to be respected in that case, not the full range.

## Dropping down to frame the trade

Once the EQ is marked, go to the **1H or 30M** and look for the key level there — a gap being the usual one. Then:

1. 10:00 opens and trades into that level.
2. SMT confirms the tap. **One stage is enough** — see [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]].
3. Take the change-in-delivery entry on the aligned lower timeframe (see [[PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs]] — 30M pairs to 3M, 15M pairs to 1M).

If the SMT is not present at the moment of the tap, wait for it to form inside the level rather than entering without it.

## When there is no SMT on the 1H or 30M

An escalation ladder rather than an abandoned trade:

1. A **PSP** on the 1H or 30M.
2. A **15M previous-candle SMT**.
3. A **PSP on the 15M** — all assets take the previous candle's low, but one closes bullish while a correlated asset closes bearish. That is a valid swing confirmation.

**If you end up on the 15M, require a two-stage SMT.** The 15M aligns to the 1M, and that execution timeframe is too fine to trust on a single divergence. This is the condition under which dropping to the 15M is legitimate — as opposed to hunting the 15M for any random swing, which is not.

## If 10:00 opens and immediately expands

There is no entry at the open, but the profile is not dead. **As long as the draw is still open**, wait for 10:00 to *create* a new key level after it displaces away. 11:00 or 12:00 then taps that level, and you trade the tap as the continuation. You are still trading the 10:00 continuation even though the entry lands in a later candle.

## Wick too large on the entry candle

If the candle you would be entering from has too large a wick to work with, wait for the next one to open and take the continuation sequence off that instead. Same principle as the 4H small-wick filter, applied to the execution timeframe.

## Change in delivery — the three entry signatures

1. **Stop run into change in delivery.** Price runs a low, then V-shapes back.
2. **SMT into change in delivery.** Price fails to take the low a correlated asset takes, then closes above the down-close candle that set the divergence.
3. **Gap into change in delivery.** Price trades into a gap, then closes above the down-close candles that formed it.

**Market in rather than limit in.** Price does not reliably come back to tap the change in delivery, so a resting limit often misses the trade entirely. If the close is far from the level and the risk is skewed, the alternative is to wait for a gap to form, then trade the tap of that gap with the stop above the swing.

Targets in the worked examples run 2R–3R, with 3R described as the usual take.

## A note on the chain

The continuation does not have to follow the *immediately* preceding reversal. A 02:00 reversal with 06:00 expanding also sets up 10:00 as the continuation — you are continuing the expansion, not strictly the last candle.

\# Asia Reversal to London Continuation

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Clock-time equivalent: [[2200 Reversal]]

## The setup

Asia puts in the **low of day** (or high of day) for the daily candle and forms a reversal signature. Asia opens, trades toward a key level, sweeps it out with a [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion|C2 candle that supports expansion]] (small wick), and reverses.

## What comes next

When Asia reverses and **leaves an open draw**, expect **London to continue** toward that draw. This mirrors [[Session Probability Map]]'s logic from the earlier framework — an early-session reversal with an unmet draw sets up the next session to finish the job.

## How to actually trade it

1. Confirm the 4H candle opens and respects the previous 50% range of its C2 candle (see [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule]]).
2. Fractalize down to find the refined key level — commonly an hourly gap sitting in the **upper quadrant** of the 4H candle (for a bullish continuation).
3. Wait for price to trade into that gap with a small, supportive C2-style wick.
4. Expand away from the gap toward the open draw.

\# London Reversal to New York Continuation

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Clock-time equivalent: [[0200 Reversal]]

## The setup

This one shows up when **Asia consolidates** — it doesn't take a key level itself. London then opens, manipulates a key level, and expands away, forming the high or low of day.

## What comes next

If London **takes** its draw on liquidity, the session's done. But if London reverses and **doesn't** take that draw, expect **06:00 or New York open** to come and finish the move. This is called one of the easiest frameworks to trade in this whole system.

## How to actually trade it

The only thing to look for is a **gap continuation** off the refined key level of the previous 4H candle:

1. The prior 4H candle has already expanded.
2. The new 4H candle opens inside a refined key level.
3. An hourly fractal still supports expansion — a small closing run trading into the gap, with an open draw still unmet.
4. Expand from there toward the open draw.

\# New York Manipulation Reversal (Early NY)

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Clock-time equivalent: [[0600 Reversal]]

## The setup

Asia and London both tend to **consolidate** — neither takes a key level of its own — and **early New York** (the 06:00 candle) is the one that finally manipulates a key level and expands toward strong liquidity.

## The alignment requirement

This profile leans hard on [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)|fractal alignment]]: the daily candle, the 4H candle, and the 1H candle should all show small wicks supporting expansion in the same direction. Each profile has to align since price is fractal — this is described as especially key for this specific setup.

## How to actually trade it

1. The 06:00 candle manipulates the key level with a small, supportive wick and reverses away.
2. Assuming an open draw remains, the next candle (10:00) opens and respects the previous 50% of that candle's range, landing inside a refined key level (commonly an hourly gap).
3. A small opposing run forms there, and price expands higher toward the open draw liquidity.

\# New York Reversal to 2PM Continuation

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Clock-time equivalent: [[1000 Reversal - Expansion]], [[1400 - No Trade]]

## The setup

This is when **10:00** actually forms the high or low of day: it opens, sweeps a key level, reverses, and expands away — with a small wick that supports the expansion.

## What comes next: a conditional 2pm continuation

If 10:00 leaves an **open draw** rather than reaching it fully, you can frame a **14:00 continuation**: 14:00 opens inside a refined key level (the same mechanic as every other profile in this section) and continues toward the open draw, provided 10:00 didn't already take it.

## Reconciling this with "2pm is not traded"

The earlier, lighter framework ([[1400 - No Trade]]) treats 14:00 as excluded entirely because the session itself is slow and lethargic. This deeper framework refines that: 14:00 isn't a profile-generating candle **on its own**, but it can still passively **continue** an already-open 10:00 draw if one exists — inherited momentum from the 10:00 setup, not a fresh 14:00 profile. The two notes agree on the core point (don't expect 14:00 to originate anything); this one just adds the specific mechanism for how a leftover 10:00 draw plays out if it does continue into 14:00.

## How to actually trade it

1. Confirm 10:00 is a valid reversal-to-expansion candle (small wick, key level taken).
2. If an open draw remains, wait for 14:00 to open inside a refined key level (as shown in every other profile in this section).
3. Trade the continuation from there toward the open draw.

\# Entry Discount vs. Premium Rule

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · See also [[Stop Placement - Body vs Wick]]

## The rule

Never enter so far into a range that your stop ends up sitting deep in **premium** (or deep discount, for a short). You always want your stop to remain near the **discount** of the current range you're trading within — regardless of how good the entry trigger itself looks.

## How to define "the current range"

Mark the **current low and current high** of the range you're actually trading inside of — not the whole day's range, just the local structure relevant to this trade. Discount and premium are judged relative to that local range, not the broader session.

## Why this matters

An entry that's technically valid (a confirmed SMT, a clean retracement into a gap) can still be a poor trade if it's positioned so deep into the range that the stop has to sit in premium territory to accommodate it. That combination — good trigger, bad location — is exactly the trap this rule is meant to prevent. The entry trigger tells you *whether* to trade; this rule governs *where within the range* that trade is actually acceptable.

## Worked example
- [[Example 3 - C3 Continuation Off a Refined Key Level]] — the entry taken there keeps the stop near discount of the range, explicitly marked out on the current low/high

\# Stop Placement — Body vs. Wick

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]]

## The rule

Where you place your stop depends on the **composition of the candle** your entry is anchored to:

- If the candle is **mostly body**, put your stop at the **bodies**.
- If the candle is **mostly wick**, put your stop at the **wick**.

## Why

A candle that's mostly body represents a decisive, committed move — the bodies are the meaningful structure, and a stop placed there respects that the wick beyond it was likely just a brief, low-significance poke. A candle that's mostly wick tells the opposite story — the wick itself *is* the significant structure (that's where the SMT/rejection happened), so the stop needs to sit beyond the wick to respect it.

## How to apply it

Look at the entry candle (typically the 3-minute or 5-minute V-shape reversal signature you entered on) and judge its composition directly: does the real body dominate the range, or does the wick? Place the stop accordingly, rather than defaulting to "always beyond the wick" or "always beyond the body."

## Worked example
- [[Example 2 - Two-Stage SMT Reversal with 3-5 Minute Entry]] — entry near the close of a strong V-shape, stop placed at the bodies since the entry candle was mostly body

\# Example 1 — Top-Down Fractal Alignment Filter

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Concept: [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)]]

## Working top-down

Starting on the **daily** chart: a small wick supports expansion in the intended direction. Assuming price has traded into a key level, the **4H** shows a [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion|C2 reversal-to-expansion candle]] — small wick, supports expansion higher.

## The filter catches something

Fractalizing down to the **hourly**: the candle you're actually trading *within* does **not** support expansion — it has a large wick. Even though the daily and 4H both look valid, this hourly candle fails the alignment check.

## What that means for execution

Don't trade this hourly C2 candle. Let it close, and trade **C3** instead — exactly the same [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion|large-wick rule]] applied one layer further down the fractal chain. On the lower timeframe, this looks like: an initial reversal signature forms (the one to skip), then C3 opens and forms a clean continuation signature — that clean C3 signature is where you'd actually position.

## The alternate branch — when the hourly *does* align

If instead the hourly candle you're trading within also supports expansion (small wick, same direction as daily and 4H), this is when you trade the 4H reversal directly: position yourself in the **lower quadrant** of that candle's width, waiting for price to **V-shape away** with a strong close. A lackluster or hesitant reversal here is not good enough — see [[Valid Reversal Signatures (The V-Shape)]].

## Takeaway

This is the practical demonstration of [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)]]: a valid daily and 4H read is not sufficient on its own — the hourly candle you're actually entering within has to pass the same small-wick test, or you wait one more candle.

\# Example 2 — Two-Stage SMT Reversal with 3–5 Minute Entry

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Concepts: [[Two-Stage Cracks for Reversals]], [[Stop Placement - Body vs Wick]]

## 4H setup

On the H4 chart: price (C1) trades into a key level and forms SMT there — the **first-stage crack**, since the correlated asset does not take this low.

## The two-stage confirmation

- **Stage 1**: at the key level itself (C1), the correlated asset fails to take the low.
- **Stage 2**: C2 opens lower, sweeps C1's low, and forms its own crack at that same low — again, a correlated asset does not take this candle's low while the traded asset does.

Both stages are now confirmed. This candle also has a **small wick**, which supports expansion — so the plan is to expand away from this two-stage SMT rather than waiting for a later candle.

## Fractal alignment down

Refining to the **hourly**: the aligned candle also supports expansion (small wick, same low, same direction) — everything is aligning per [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)]].

## The entry — 3 or 5 minute

The only thing left is a clean lower-timeframe reversal signature. Off of the SMT, price should **V-shape away** — taking one or two candles to fully commit, followed by a strong move. Entry is taken **near the close** of that V-shape.

## Stop placement

Stop goes **at the bodies** here (not the wick), because the entry candle is mostly body — see [[Stop Placement - Body vs Wick]]. Hold for the open draw.

## Takeaway

This is the fullest version of the two-stage reversal process in this framework: key level → stage 1 crack → C2 sweep → stage 2 crack → small wick confirms expansion → hourly alignment confirms → 3/5-minute V-shape gives the actual entry, with a body-based stop.

\# Example 3 — C3 Continuation Off a Refined Key Level

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Concepts: [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]], [[Entry Discount vs Premium Rule]]

## Why C2 is skipped

The C2 candle here has a **very large wick** — per [[C2 Closures That Support vs Don't Support Expansion]], this candle is not tradable. The plan shifts immediately to trading **C3** instead.

## C3's setup

C3 opens with a **small opposing run**. Fractalizing down to the hourly/30-minute chart: price is retracing into a **refined key level** — a gap. SMT (or "SMT fill") is present at that gap — this only requires a **one-stage crack**, since it's a continuation off a fair value gap rather than a reversal off a key level. See [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]].

## Fractal alignment

That hourly candle also has a small wick, supporting expansion to the upside — so this passes [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)|the alignment filter]] the same way any other setup does.

## The entry

On the lower timeframe: there's still an open draw, and price is **V-shaping away** from the gap, heading toward it.

## The trade management lesson

The entry taken here keeps the **stop near discount of the range** — not entered so deep into the range that the stop would sit in premium. The current low and current high of the trading range are explicitly marked to judge this. See [[Entry Discount vs Premium Rule]].

## Takeaway

This is the clean template for "I can't trade C2, so I trade C3 instead": large wick disqualifies C2 → refined key level (gap) found on the hourly → one-stage crack confirms → alignment holds → V-shape entry with a discount-respecting stop.

\# Example 4 — C4 Continuation After Invalid C2 and C3

← [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] · Concept: [[When C2 and C3 Both Fail to Manipulate (The C4 Case)]]

## Setup

Neither C2 nor C3 cleanly manipulates a previous wick here. Instead of the standard triplet, the confirmed reversal signature doesn't show up until later in the sequence — pushing the tradable continuation one candle further out than usual, onto what this framework labels **C4**.

## The execution method doesn't change

This is explicitly the **same framework** as a standard C3 continuation — a [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule|refined key level]] within the fractal timeframe is what actually forms the higher-timeframe candle's wick:

1. The 4H candle opens.
2. On the 1H/30M, price trades lower (or higher) into a refined key level — a fair value gap.
3. A small-wick candle forms there, supporting expansion.
4. Assuming an open draw still exists, the continuation plays out from there.

## Takeaway

The specific candle label (C3 vs. C4) matters less than the underlying principle: however many candles it takes for a genuinely valid reversal signature to show up, the same refined-key-level mechanic is what you use to trade the continuation once it does. Don't force an entry just because "C2" or "C3" technically printed — wait for the candle that actually satisfies [[Valid Reversal Signatures (The V-Shape)|the validity filter]], whichever position in the sequence it happens to occupy.

\# Candle Profiling — Complete Framework

This is the **master hub** — the most in-depth, most complete breakdown of the profiling concept in this vault. It covers the same underlying territory as [[4H Profiling]], [[1H-30M Alignment to 4H Profile]], and [[Combining them]], but goes considerably deeper: the foundational C2/C3 closure logic, what makes a reversal signature valid vs. invalid, the fractal alignment filter across daily/4H/1H, the refined-key-level execution mechanic, one-stage vs. two-stage cracking correlation (SMT), and concrete trade management (stop placement, entry location).

**Use this as your primary reference.** The other three folders remain useful as the original, lighter-weight versions of related ideas — see [[How This Relates to the Other Vault Sections]] below — but this is the one to come back to for the full picture.

---

## 1. Foundations
The base filter every profile has to pass before anything else matters.

- [[What Is Candle Profiling]]

## 2. Reversal Signature Validity
The visual filter for telling a real reversal from noise.

- [[Valid Reversal Signatures (The V-Shape)]]
- [[Invalid Reversal Signatures (Two-Sided Consolidation)]]

## 3. Fractal Alignment
The core execution mechanic — how a 4H idea becomes an actual lower-timeframe entry.

- [[The Fractal Alignment Filter (Daily, 4H, 1H)]]
- [[The Refined Key Level and the 50% Open Rule]]
- [[Intracandle Continuation (Universal Model)]]

## 4. Cracking Correlation (SMT)
- [[Two-Stage Cracks for Reversals]]
- [[One-Stage Cracks for Continuations]]

## 5. Session Profiles
The daily cycle, named by session instead of clock time.

- [[Asia Reversal to London Continuation]]
- [[London Reversal to New York Continuation]]
- [[New York Manipulation Reversal (Early NY)]]
- [[New York Reversal to 2PM Continuation]]

## 6. Trade Management

- [[Stop Placement - Body vs Wick]]
- [[Entry Discount vs Premium Rule]]

## 7. Worked Examples

- [[Example 1 - Top-Down Fractal Alignment Filter]]
- [[Example 2 - Two-Stage SMT Reversal with 3-5 Minute Entry]]
- [[Example 3 - C3 Continuation Off a Refined Key Level]]
- [[Example 4 - C4 Continuation After Invalid C2 and C3]]

---

## The One-Sentence Version

> Candle profiling starts with whether C2's closure supports expansion (small wick) or doesn't (large wick, wait for C3) — and every trade after that has to pass three more filters: a real key level plus an open draw, a valid V-shaped reversal signature, and fractal alignment across daily/4H/1H — before you drop down to a refined key level for the actual entry.

## How This Relates to the Other Vault Sections

| This framework's term | Equivalent in the older notes |
|---|---|
| C2 closure supports expansion (small wick) | [[Wick Size Rule]], [[Small Wick Requirement for C2]] |
| Two-stage crack | [[Two-Stage SMT for the Reversal Candle]] |
| One-stage crack | The SMT used in [[Continuation Entry - Gap Method]] |
| Refined key level | The gap in [[The Wick-in-Gap Alignment Setup]] |
| Fractal alignment filter | [[HTF to LTF Transition Mindset]], but extended down to the **daily** candle too |
| Asia / London / New York sessions | [[4H Session Map]]'s 18:00–22:00 / 02:00–06:00 / 06:00–10:00–14:00 clock windows — see [[Timestamp Reference Sheet]] |
| C4 | An extension beyond [[Combining them]] for when neither C1's nor C2's wick actually manipulates the key level |

The older notes are still accurate — they're just the earlier, less detailed pass. When the two disagree on emphasis, treat this framework as the refined version.

# Phases of Price

Central hub for the four phases every price cycle moves through: **consolidation, expansion, retracement, and reversal.** Each phase sets up the next — a market consolidates, manipulates one side of the range, expands away from it, retraces shallowly, expands again, and eventually that expansion meets an opposing expansion and reverses.

---

## 1. Consolidation
Tight range, internal to a high and a low — occurs after a large expansion or after a key level is hit without an immediate reversal.

- [[Trading Consolidations]]

## 2. Expansion
A large move in a single direction, born from sweeping one side of a consolidation and confirming a change in delivery.

- [[Trading Expansions]]

## 3. Retracement
A shallow, slow pullback into a gap after an expansion, before expansion resumes.

- [[Trading Retracements]]

## 4. Reversal
Expansion met with an opposing expansion after a higher-timeframe key level is hit.

- [[Trading Reversals]]

---

## How the phases connect

| Phase | Trigger | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Consolidation | Price ranges between an internal high/low | A side to eventually sweep |
| Expansion | One side of the range is swept + change in delivery | A large directional move, confirmed HTF swing |
| Retracement | Expansion pauses | A shallow pullback into a key level/gap before continuation |
| Reversal | Expansion meets an opposing expansion | Direction changes |

# Consolidation as a Continuation Signature

← [[Trading Consolidations]]

## The core idea

When price hits a key level (gap, or old high/low) and **doesn't reverse away from it immediately**, that hesitation — the consolidation itself — is a **continuation signature**, not indecision to be ignored. The expectation flips to: wait for the *opposite* side of the small range to be manipulated, then continue in the original direction.

## Why this matters

It's tempting to read "price hit my level and stalled" as a sign of weakness or reversal. Instead, treat it as the market building the next leg: it needs to manipulate one more side of the newly formed internal range before it can deliver toward the original draw on liquidity.

## What it looks like

1. Expansion into a key level.
2. Failure to reverse away — price prints an internal high and low instead (consolidation).
3. Purge of the side of the range **opposite** the original direction (e.g., after an expansion higher stalls, the *low* of the small range gets purged).
4. Change in delivery off that purge.
5. Continuation in the original direction.

## Recognizing it as an inside bar

On a higher timeframe, this consolidation can be as subtle as a single **inside bar** — a candle that stays within the prior candle's range. Don't dismiss it just because the higher-timeframe candle looks uneventful; drop to a lower timeframe to see the internal high/low structure and trade the manipulation once it happens.

## Related
- [[What Is Consolidation]]
- [[How to Trade Consolidation]]
- [[Multi-Timeframe Consolidation Workflow]]

# How to Trade Consolidation

← [[Trading Consolidations]]

## The rule: don't

While price is internal to the consolidation high and low, **do not engage.** There's no edge inside the range — you wait for one of two things to happen at the extremes.

## What you're waiting for

1. **Purge one side of the range and reverse away from it.** Take the consolidation high (or low), then reverse back into and through the range — that reversal is your signal to engage.
2. **SMT one side of the range.** A correlated asset diverges at the consolidation high or low (takes it out while the asset you're trading doesn't, or vice versa) — that divergence is also a valid trigger to engage.

Either the manipulation (purge + reversal) or the SMT can trigger engagement — you don't need both, though seeing both together adds confidence.

## Confirmation: CISD / change in delivery

The actual engagement trigger is a **change in delivery** — a V-shape reversal that closes back through the opposing candles after the purge or SMT. This is what turns "we took out the low" into "the low is now a protected swing and we can trade higher," matching the [[Protected Highs|protected-swing]] anatomy used throughout the vault.

## Bullish and bearish

- **Bullish engagement**: consolidation low purged (or SMT'd) → change in delivery (V-shape reversal, close above down-close candles) → protected low → look to trade higher.
- **Bearish engagement**: consolidation high purged (or SMT'd) → change in delivery (V-shape reversal, close below up-close candles) → protected high → look to trade lower.

## Related
- [[What Is Consolidation]]
- [[Consolidation as a Continuation Signature]]
- [[Multi-Timeframe Consolidation Workflow]]

# Multi-Timeframe Consolidation Workflow

← [[Trading Consolidations]]

## The workflow

1. **Note the higher-timeframe key level or expansion** that price is reacting to (a daily gap, a previous-day high/low, an SMT with a correlated asset).
2. **Watch the tap.** Does price reverse away from the level immediately, or stall? A stall = consolidation forming.
3. **Drop to a lower timeframe** to see the internal high/low of the consolidation clearly — it's often invisible or looks like a single inside bar on the parent timeframe.
4. **Wait for a purge of one side** of that internal range — don't engage while price is still between the high and low.
5. **Confirm with a change in delivery** (V-shape reversal, close through the opposing candles) off the purge. SMT on a correlated asset at the same extreme adds confluence but isn't required if the manipulation + change in delivery is clean on its own.
6. **Trade toward the objective** — the original draw on liquidity implied by the higher-timeframe expansion or key level (e.g., previous-day high/low, a further gap).

## Correlated-asset nuance

The same consolidation can resolve differently across correlated instruments — one may fully take out the consolidation high while another only SMTs it (wicks through without closing beyond). Either is a valid trigger; check the correlated asset when the instrument you're trading doesn't give a clean purge.

## Don't force it

Not every stall needs to be forced into a trade. If price is choppy without a clear internal high/low, or the purge-and-reversal hasn't happened yet, the correct action is to keep waiting — consolidation is explicitly the "don't trade yet" phase until one side is taken and reversed.

## Related
- [[What Is Consolidation]]
- [[How to Trade Consolidation]]
- [[Consolidation as a Continuation Signature]]

# What Is Consolidation

← [[Trading Consolidations]]

## Definition

Consolidation is **internal price action** — price gets stuck moving between an internal high and an internal low, not making meaningful progress in either direction. It's the phase everything else in the [[Phases of Price]] framework sets up from or resolves into.

## When to expect it

Two triggers:

1. **After a large expansion.** A strong directional run tends to pause and consolidate before the next move.
2. **After a key level is hit.** Tapping a gap or an old high/low and *not* immediately reversing away from it is itself the signal you're heading into consolidation.

## What it means

- If a key level is hit and price does **not** reverse away from it right away, expect **consolidation → continuation.** The consolidation is a pause, not a change of direction — it's actually a continuation signature.
- Price prints a high, prints a low, and sits internal to both — engineering liquidity on both sides until one side gets purged.

## Bullish and bearish shape

- **Bullish**: large expansion higher (or key level hit) → price prints a high and low → sits internal to the range → wait for a manipulation of the low to continue higher.
- **Bearish**: large expansion lower (or key level hit) → price prints a low and high → sits internal to the range → wait for a manipulation of the high to continue lower.

## Related
- [[How to Trade Consolidation]]
- [[Consolidation as a Continuation Signature]]

# Bearish Expansion Anatomy

← [[Trading Expansions]]

> 🎥 [Watch: bearish expansion walkthrough](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=117) (1:57–2:48), continued at [3:47](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=227)

## Setup

Tight range (consolidation) → the **high** of the range is manipulated (swept) → price reverses and expands downward.

## Step-by-step sequence

1. **Manipulate the high.** Price pushes above the consolidation high.
2. **Change in delivery.** Price expands back down through the up-close candles, closing below them — that's the reversal signature.
3. **Shallow retracement — but no key level tapped.** This is the key difference from the bullish case: the pullback does *not* tap into an existing key level, so these retracement candles are **not order blocks**.
4. **A gap opens up instead**, and the shallow retracement moves into that fresh gap rather than a pre-existing level.
5. **Expansion continues through it**, closing through the candles that tapped the gap — that closure protects the high.

Pattern in short: **manipulate high → expand → shallow retracement into a newly-opened gap → expand → shallow retracement into a gap → expand.**

## Bullish vs. bearish distinction

| | Bullish expansion | Bearish expansion |
|---|---|---|
| Swept | Consolidation low | Consolidation high |
| Direction | Up | Down |
| Retracement target | Pre-existing key level (order block) | Freshly opened gap (no prior key level) |
| Confirms | Protected low | Protected high |

## Trade engagement

Look for: sweep of the consolidation **high**, reversal (change in delivery / V-shape), then continuation into the **low** side of the range. Same lower-timeframe confirmation approach as the bullish case — drop down a timeframe to find the change-in-delivery signature at the sweep.

## Related
- [[What Is Expansion]]
- [[The Higher-Timeframe Swing Formation]]
- [[Bullish Expansion Anatomy]]

# Bullish Expansion Anatomy

← [[Trading Expansions]]

> 🎥 [Watch: bullish expansion walkthrough](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=169) (2:49–3:36) — order-block sequence explained at [1:18](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=78)

## Setup

Tight range (consolidation) → the **low** of the range is manipulated (swept) → price reverses and expands upward.

## Step-by-step sequence

1. **Manipulate the low.** Price dips below the consolidation low.
2. **Change in delivery.** Price expands back up through a run of down-close candles, closing above them. That closure is what protects this low — it should not get invalidated afterward.
3. **Tap a key level.** The expansion move taps into a key level — commonly a gap — before continuing.
4. **Close above the down-close candles** that make up that gap/level. This forms a **continuation order block**, and price expands through it.
5. **Rebalance a gap**, close above the down-close candle inside it, expand away again.

Pattern in short: **manipulate low → expand → shallow retracement into a key level (order block) → expand → shallow retracement into a key level → expand.**

## What confirms continuation

- Each shallow retracement should tap an **order block** (a location tied to a key level / opposing candles) — not just any pullback.
- Each subsequent close through the down-close candles reinforces the protected low and confirms the up-move is still intact.
- Equal highs forming along the way tend to get taken (liquidity draw) before the next leg of expansion — don't mistake that sweep for a reversal.

## Trade engagement

Look for: sweep of the consolidation **low**, reversal (change in delivery / V-shape) back into the range, then continuation into the **high** side. Confirmation comes from dropping to a lower timeframe and finding the same change-in-delivery signature at the sweep point.

# The Higher-Timeframe Swing Formation

← [[Trading Expansions]]

> 🎥 [Watch: HTF swing formation explained](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=53) (0:53–1:17), continued in the [chart walkthrough](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=169) (2:49–4:21)

## The core idea

Whenever price takes out a **consolidation low or consolidation high**, it is printing a **swing point on the higher timeframe** — and expansion is the move away from that newly-printed HTF swing.

Consolidation on the HTF chart = a tight range internal to a high and a low. When the lower timeframe sweeps one side of that range and reverses, it's putting in the HTF swing formation (a higher timeframe low or high) at the same time it kicks off the expansion.

## How to identify it

Look for **opposing candles** — a change in delivery:

1. Price sweeps the consolidation low/high (manipulation).
2. Price expands through a run of opposing-color candles (e.g., closing back above down-close candles after a low sweep).
3. That closure often taps into a **key level** first — commonly a gap.
4. The close through the opposing candles is the **change in delivery**, and it leaves those candles as a **protected swing**.

This is the same anatomy covered in [[Protected Highs]] — a key level or SMT, a reversal, and an aligned-timeframe close through opposing candles to confirm. Expansion is what that confirmed swing does next: it drives price away from the level in one direction.

## Why it matters

Once the HTF swing is confirmed (protected), you have a directional bias: the expansion should keep making shallow retracements into gaps/order blocks and closing through opposing candles on the way, without giving back the protected swing. If the protected swing gets violated, the expansion read is invalidated.

- [[Bullish Expansion Anatomy]]
- [[Bearish Expansion Anatomy]]
- [[Protected Highs]]

# Trading Engagement Rules

← [[Trading Expansions]]

> 🎥 Chart examples: [hourly chart](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=271) (4:31–6:20) · [YM, consolidation → expansion](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=381) (6:21–9:38) · [15-minute, order-block chain](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=579) (9:39–13:41)

## The setup you're looking for

You want to see one side of a range purged, then the reversal carry through to the other side:

- **Sweep the low → expand to the high** (bullish read), or
- **Sweep the high → expand to the low** (bearish read).

Being "internal" to a prior high and a prior low (price sitting back inside a range after tagging both extremes at different times) is the cue to start watching for which side gets swept next and which direction the expansion will run.

## The confirmation workflow

1. **Mark the range** — the internal high and internal low you're consolidating between.
2. **Wait for a sweep** of one side.
3. **Drop to a lower timeframe** at the sweep point and look for a **change in delivery** — a close through the opposing candles, ideally with a **V-shape reversal**. This is what turns the sweep into a valid **[[Protected Highs|protected swing]]**, not just noise.
4. **Track the shallow retracements** as expansion continues: each one should tap a gap or order block, then close through the opposing candles to keep expanding. Deep retracements or a failure to close through the opposing candles is a warning sign the expansion is stalling.
5. **Watch for liquidity draws along the way** — equal highs/lows forming mid-expansion tend to get taken before the next leg continues; that's a pause, not a reversal, as long as the protected swing behind you holds.
6. **Protection holding = stay in the expansion.** If the protected low (bullish case) or protected high (bearish case) gets violated, the expansion thesis is invalidated — reassess rather than assume continuation.

## Multi-timeframe note

This read works the same way on any timeframe — hourly, 15-minute, or lower. The pattern is scale-invariant: consolidation → sweep → HTF swing formation → drop a timeframe → change in delivery → expansion with shallow retracements.

# What Is Expansion

← [[Trading Expansions]]

> 🎥 [Watch: definition + bullish/bearish overview](https://youtu.be/cqc9AS_XCVc?t=19) (0:19–2:56)

## Definition

Expansion is a **large move in the market in a single direction**. It's one of the four [[Phases of Price]], and it shows up in one specific spot in the sequence: **after consolidation, or after retracement.**

- Consolidation → expansion
- Expansion → shallow retracement → expansion (repeat)

## How a consolidation turns into an expansion

A consolidation is a tight range with an internal high and an internal low. You leave that consolidation by:

1. **Taking out the low or the high** of the range (the manipulation/purge), then
2. **Moving in the opposing direction** — that reversal away from the purge *is* the expansion.

So the sequence is: tight range → purge one side → large move the other way → small retracement → large move again → small retracement → large move again.

## Bullish vs. bearish expansion

- **Bullish expansion**: consolidation → the **low** of the range is manipulated (swept) → price expands upward away from it.
- **Bearish expansion**: consolidation → the **high** of the range is manipulated (swept) → price expands downward away from it.

## The tell: shallow retracements

Once you're in an expansion, the retracements against the move stay **shallow** — small wicks, not deep pullbacks. Big move, small wick, big move, small wick. If retracements start getting deep instead of shallow, that's the signal expansion may be giving way to the next phase ([[Phases of Price|retracement or reversal]]).

## Related
- [[The Higher-Timeframe Swing Formation]]
- [[Bullish Expansion Anatomy]]
- [[Bearish Expansion Anatomy]]

# Multi-Timeframe Retracement Workflow

← [[Trading Retracements]]

## The workflow

1. **Identify the expansion** on the timeframe you're trading, and note where it opened gaps — those gaps are the eventual retracement targets, and the objective (draw on liquidity) beyond them.
2. **Watch the reaction after a key level is tapped or a HTF swing forms** (e.g., a 30-minute swing formation, or SMT on a correlated asset). If price fails to reverse cleanly, expect a retracement rather than a reversal.
3. **Drop to a lower timeframe** to see the retracement clearly — on the parent timeframe it can look like nothing (or even like a small consolidation/inside bar); on the lower timeframe it's a distinct slow, shallow move into a gap.
4. **Compare speeds explicitly**: the move that created the expansion vs. the move that's retracing. Slow-back-out after fast-in is the retracement tell (see [[Retracement vs. Reversal]]).
5. **Wait for closure through the opposing candles** that tapped the retracement's gap — that's what confirms the retracement is complete and price is going back into expansion.
6. **Target continuation** in the original direction, through the failure swings the retracement built up.

## SMT as confirmation

Retracements often coincide with an **SMT** (correlated-asset divergence) at the gap/level the retracement is tapping into — e.g., one index takes out a low while the correlated index does not. This adds confidence that the pullback is a retracement (continuation setup) rather than the start of a reversal.

## Consolidation can hide a retracement

On a higher timeframe, a retracement can look like nothing more than a small consolidation or an inside bar — price barely moves. Dropping down a timeframe (or several) reveals the actual shallow retracement-into-gap structure underneath. Don't dismiss a quiet higher-timeframe candle; check the lower timeframe before assuming there's nothing tradable there.

- [[What Is a Retracement]]
- [[Retracement Anatomy]]
- [[Retracement vs. Reversal]]
- [[Trading Expansions]]

# Retracement Anatomy

← [[Trading Retracements]]

## The full sequence

1. **Tight range**, purge one side (the same [[The Higher-Timeframe Swing Formation|consolidation-to-expansion]] trigger).
2. **Expansion away**, closing through the opposing-color candles (down-close for bullish, up-close for bearish).
3. **Shallow, slow pullback** — this is the retracement. It builds up minor structure (failure swings) on the side it pulls back toward, and drifts into a **gap**.
4. **Closure through the opposing candles that tapped the gap** — this confirms the retracement is done and price is going back into expansion.
5. **Expansion away again.**

Pattern in short: **manipulate → expand → shallow/slow retracement into a gap → close through opposing candles → expand → repeat.**

## Bullish version

Tight range → take out the low → expand away closing above down-close candles → shallow pullback into a gap → close above the down-close candles in that gap → expand away from the low again.

## Bearish version

Tight range → take out the high → expand away closing below up-close candles → shallow pullback into a gap building failure swings above → close below the up-close candles that traded into the gap → expand away again.

## The failure swings detail

During the pullback, minor highs/lows (failure swings) build up on the side price is retracing toward. These get run through once the next expansion leg starts — they aren't levels to trade against on their own (see [[Failure Swings]] in the reversals notes).

## Related
- [[What Is a Retracement]]
- [[Retracement vs. Reversal]]
- [[Multi-Timeframe Retracement Workflow]]

# Retracement vs. Reversal

← [[Trading Retracements]]

## The distinguishing test: speed and depth

Both a retracement and a [[Trading Reversals|reversal]] can start the same way — a pullback after an expansion, into a key level. What separates them:

| | Retracement | Reversal |
|---|---|---|
| Speed back | Slow, lethargic | Fast — matches or approaches the speed of the original expansion |
| Depth | Shallow | Can be deep, and takes out the swing that framed the move |
| Structure produced | Failure swings, minor highs/lows | A genuine opposing expansion (expansion met with expansion) |
| Net effect | Continuation of the prior direction | Change in the prevailing direction |

**Fast in, slow back out → retracement, expect continuation. Fast in, fast back out → potential reversal.**

## In practice

If price taps a key level and the reaction away from it is sluggish and shallow, treat it as a retracement — the higher-timeframe direction hasn't actually changed, and you should be looking to get on side with the original move once the retracement completes (closure through the opposing candles). Only when the move away from the level is itself expansion-fast should you start framing a reversal instead.

## Related
- [[What Is a Retracement]]
- [[Retracement Anatomy]]
- [[Trading Reversals]]

# What Is a Retracement

← [[Trading Retracements]]

## Definition

A retracement is a **shallow, slow pullback** — a move in the opposite direction to the draw on liquidity, after an [[Trading Expansions|expansion]]. It happens **after expansion**: expand → retrace → expand.

## What makes it a retracement (not a reversal)

Two qualities give it away:

- **Shallow** — it doesn't travel far. It builds up minor structure (failure swings) instead of taking out anything significant.
- **Slow** — the pace of the move back is noticeably slower/more lethargic than the expansion that preceded it.

Compare the speed of the move into a level against the speed of the move away from it: **fast in, slow back out = retracement. Fast in, fast back out = potential [[Trading Reversals|reversal]]** (expansion met with expansion). This speed comparison is the fastest way to tell the two apart in real time.

## Where it goes

A retracement pulls back into a **key level — always a gap.** It's the shallow move into that gap, followed by a closure through the opposing candles, that sets up the next expansion.

## Why it matters

If you miss the original expansion, a retracement is your next opportunity to get on side — expansions tend to repeat (expand → retrace → expand → retrace → expand), so there's usually another entry coming.

## Related
- [[Retracement vs. Reversal]]
- [[Trading Retracements]]
- [[Trading Expansions]]

# Bearish Reversal Signature

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## Setup

Market is expanding **higher**, but has **not yet hit** the key level (HTF gap or HTF old high) above it.

## Sequence

1. **Expansion higher — but the key level isn't hit yet.** This matters: without tagging the key level, you cannot frame a valid reversal signature away from this high. What follows is just a retracement, not a reversal (see [[Reversal vs. Retracement]]).
2. **Small retracement lower into a gap.**
3. **Expansion back up**, this time actually **taking out the key level and the prior high.**
4. **Watch the reaction at the key level**: displace through and continue, consolidate, or reverse?
5. **Expansion back into the range** — price reverses down through the up-close candles, printing the change in delivery: expansion (up) met with expansion (down).
6. Once this prints, treat the high as a **protected high** and target the downside objective (lows to the left).

## The critical distinction

The first leg up in this example does **not** count as a reversal setup because it never reached the key level. Only once the key level is actually tagged can the subsequent expansion-into-expansion be read as a valid reversal.

## Related
- [[What Is a Reversal]]
- [[Bullish Reversal Signature]]
- [[Reversal vs. Retracement]]

# Bullish Reversal Signature

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## Setup

Market is expanding **lower** into a key level (HTF gap or HTF old low).

## Sequence

1. **Expansion into the key level.** Price drives down into the gap/old low.
2. **Failed reversal / small retracement.** Often the first reaction is just a small retracement, not a real reversal — don't jump the gun here.
3. **Expansion again below the low.** Price pushes below that low, tapping deeper into or through the key level.
4. **Expansion back into the range.** Price snaps back up through the down-close candles — this is the **change in delivery**: expansion (down) met with expansion (up).
5. Once this prints, treat the low as a **protected low** and target the **highs to the left** as the objective.

## What to watch for at the key level

Ask specifically: after price hits the key level, does it —
- **Displace straight through and continue** (no reversal — this is continuation, not reversal), or
- **Consolidate**, then manipulate and expand back into the range (the reversal signature), or
- **Reverse immediately** with a clean V-shape?

Only the last two count as a valid reversal setup; watch for which one is playing out before assuming direction.

## Related
- [[What Is a Reversal]]
- [[Bearish Reversal Signature]]
- [[Reversal vs. Retracement]]

# Failure Swings

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## What they are

A failure swing is a small, low-conviction high or low left behind as price runs through a series of minor levels on its way to a real objective — equal highs/lows, minor wicks, and other structure that gets swept without producing its own reversal. They're the debris of a strong expansion, not standalone reversal points.

## The rule: don't trade against them

**You don't want to be trading against failure swings.** Even if a small pullback at a failure swing *looks* like a clean setup, it isn't one to fade — the higher-timeframe context is still driving price through it.

## How to tell a failure swing from a real level

Ask what the higher timeframe is actually showing:

- Is there a real **higher-timeframe gap** (1H, 30M, etc.) at this level?
- Is this printing a genuine **higher-timeframe wick** (a level the HTF chart is rejecting from), or just a minor internal high/low on the timeframe you're zoomed into?

If the higher timeframe doesn't confirm the level as significant, treat it as a failure swing to be run through, not a level to reverse from. Only trade reversals from confirmed **key levels** (see [[What Is a Reversal]]) — not every wick that looks like resistance.

## In practice

In an active reversal/expansion, you'll often see a whole chain of failure swings between your entry and your real objective (e.g., a distant high or low). The correct read is to expect those to get run through on the way to the objective — not to treat each one as its own trade.

## Related
- [[What Is a Reversal]]
- [[Reversal vs. Retracement]]
- [[Multi-Timeframe Reversal Workflow]]

# Multi-Timeframe Reversal Workflow

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## The workflow

1. **Find the key level on the higher timeframe** — a daily/4H/1H gap, or a relevant old high/low. "Relevant" means there's real distance between it and the last time price traded there; the farther apart, the more weight the level carries as a place to expect a reaction.
2. **Align down to a lower timeframe** to actually watch the reversal signature print (see time-frame alignment — a dedicated concept covered elsewhere in the vault). The bigger the HTF level, the more timeframes you may need to step down through.
3. **Watch the reaction at the level**: continuation through it, consolidation, or a reversal signature (expansion met with expansion / change in delivery)?
4. **Once the change in delivery confirms**, mark the swing behind it as protected and set the objective — usually the nearest significant high/low, or the HTF gap/level that framed the move in the first place.
5. **Track the swing as protected all the way to the objective.** It's normal to see multiple internal change-in-delivery prints (retracement → expansion, retracement → expansion) along the way — each one should keep reinforcing the same protected swing, not invalidate it.
6. **Ignore [[Failure Swings]] along the route** — don't trade against the minor highs/lows price runs through en route to the real objective.

## SMT as an added confirmation

Some examples print an **SMT (correlated-asset divergence)** right at the key level alongside the expansion-into-expansion signature. When present, it adds confidence to the reversal read, but the core requirement is still the key level + change-in-delivery sequence — SMT is a bonus, not a replacement.

## Volatility note: market open

Around market open (e.g., New York open), volatility is elevated — step down to a lower timeframe than usual (e.g., 3-minute or 1-minute instead of 5/15-minute) to read the reversal signature cleanly during this window.

## Not every setup works

Even a textbook-looking sequence — SMT at a key level, clean change of delivery, order block continuation — can still fail. Expect some trades that fit the full signature to simply not work out; that's a normal part of applying this framework, not a sign the read was wrong.

# Reversal vs. Retracement

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## The test: has the key level been hit?

This is the single question that separates a valid reversal setup from a plain retracement:

- **Key level (HTF gap or HTF old high/low) has been tagged** → you can frame a reversal from here once expansion meets expansion.
- **Key level has *not* been tagged** → whatever pullback you're seeing is just a **retracement**, not a reversal. There is no valid reversal to frame yet.

## Why this matters

It's tempting to see a sharp move back against the trend and immediately call it a reversal. But without the key level having been met first, that move is structurally just a retracement inside the ongoing expansion — the higher-timeframe objective hasn't been reached yet, so there's no reason for the market to actually turn.

## Reading the sequence in practice

Price action is a chain of expansions and retracements, and the label for each leg depends on speed and context:

- **Fast move + slow move back** = expansion met with a retracement (not a reversal — continuation is still likely).
- **Fast move + fast move back** (roughly matching speed/character, after a key level) = expansion met with expansion → **change in delivery** → valid reversal signature.

Compare the speed of the move into the level against the speed of the move away from it. A slow grind back is a retracement; a sharp snap back is expansion.

## Worked pattern

A full reversal sequence often looks like: **expansion → retracement → expansion → retracement → expansion into the key level → expansion back into the range (reversal signature) → retracement → expansion → retracement → expansion → objective met.** Each individual leg needs to be classified on its own — don't assume the whole move is one clean reversal.

# What Is a Reversal

← [[Trading Reversals]]

## Definition

A reversal is **expansion met with expansion** — an [[Trading Expansions|expansion]] into a key level, followed by an opposing expansion back the other way. If the market is expanding lower, a reversal means it expands lower into a key level, and then expands *higher* out of it — and vice versa.

## The precondition: a key level must be met

A reversal can only be framed **after a key level has been hit.** The key levels to watch are:

- **Higher-timeframe gaps**
- **Higher-timeframe old highs and lows**

No key level tagged means no valid reversal to frame — see [[Reversal vs. Retracement]] for what price is doing instead when this precondition isn't met.

## The signature you're looking for

1. Expansion into the key level.
2. The reaction *at* the key level — this is the part to watch closely. You're asking: are we displacing straight through and continuing, consolidating, or reversing?
3. If reversing: a small retracement/manipulation at the level, then an **expansion back into the range** — this is the [[Protected Highs|change in delivery]] that confirms the reversal.

Once that change in delivery prints, the swing behind it (the key-level extreme) becomes a **protected swing**, and the objective becomes the opposing high/low — typically the highs or lows to the left.

\# Aligning Expansions Across Timeframes

← [[Protected Highs]] · Companion to [[PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs]]

## What this answers

[[PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs]] answers *"a key level was hit — which timeframe confirms the swing?"*. This answers a different question: **"which timeframe's key level forms the wick of the expansion candle I want to trade?"**

The two ladders overlap at the bottom and agree there. They are not competing tables.

## The expansion ladder

An expansion candle's **wick** has to form inside a key level from the timeframe below it:

| Expansion candle | Its wick forms inside a key level on |
|---|---|
| Daily | 4 hour |
| 4 hour | 1 hour or 30 minute |

Then the entry comes off the timeframe aligned to the level you framed:

| Key level found on | Entry signature timeframe |
|---|---|
| 1 hour | 5 minute |
| 30 minute | 3 minute |
| 15 minute | 1 minute |

Those last three are the same pairs as [[PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs]] — the ladders converge once you are down at execution.

**15M → 1M is the scalping end.** It becomes properly probable rather than a scalp when 9:30 creates a 15-minute gap, because a gap there implies expansion through the 10:00 candle.

## What counts as the key level

Either of two things, in both directions:

- a **gap**
- a **swing high or low**

If there is no gap, the wick can still form off a swing point — but the reversal away from that swing has to be real: it either **sweeps** the level, or shows **SMT** (this asset fails to take the low while a correlated one takes it), and then prints the reversal signature.

## When the candle fails to reverse on its own

If the candle trades into the level but does **not** produce the reversal there, you demand the next candle **take out the previous candle's low** (or high) first. That sweep is where the change in delivery is allowed to form. Until then there is no aligned entry.

Once that lower-timeframe reversal signature prints, the wick is **protected** — price should not take that low again. If it does, the alignment is broken.

## "Propulsion block" — vocabulary, not a new mechanic

The video calls the second entry a **propulsion block**. It is just a **CISD** — a change in delivery, the same signature as the first one ([[Change in Delivery and the V-Shape Confirmation]]). Nothing new to learn.

The only thing that differs is *when* you take it: after the first change in delivery has already printed, the next candle opens, trades back into a fresh gap left by the move, and V-shapes away from it. That is your re-entry if you missed the first — not a separate pattern, and not a reason to chase.

## Chaining the whole stack

The worked examples run the full ladder in one trade: daily expansion aligned to a 4H gap → 4H expansion aligned to a 1H gap → 1H level aligned to a 5M entry signature. Each layer only confirms the one above it; you are not re-deciding direction at each step.

Where a candle gives no clean reversal, drop one timeframe and look for a gap inside it rather than abandoning the alignment.

\# PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs

← [[Protected Highs]]

## Why this comes first

You cannot find protected swing points without timeframe alignment. Once a key level is hit, you have to know *which* lower timeframe is the one that confirms whether the swing is protected — guessing or using an arbitrary timeframe breaks the whole method.

## The PDA timeframes

When price taps an old high/low or trades into a fair value gap, the PDA (the key level itself) is identified on one of these timeframes:

**Daily · 4H · 1H · 30M · 15M**

## The aligned pairs

Once the PDA is hit, drop to the **aligned timeframe** for that PDA's timeframe to look for the confirmation ([[Change in Delivery and the V-Shape Confirmation]]):

| PDA timeframe | Aligned confirmation timeframe |
|---|---|
| Daily | 1 hour |
| 4 hour | 15 minute |
| 1 hour | 5 minute |
| 30 minute | 3 minute |
| 15 minute | 1 minute |

## How it's used in practice

The confirmation can also **chain** through intermediate timeframes: in the [[ES - 30M to 3M Chain Confirming the 1H Swing|ES example]], a 3-minute change confirms the 30-minute swing, which in turn confirms the 1-hour swing. You don't always confirm the highest timeframe directly — sometimes the intermediate timeframe confirms it for you, one aligned pair at a time.

\# Change in Delivery and the V-Shape Confirmation

← [[Protected Highs]] · See also [[What Creates a Protected Swing]]

## What "change in delivery" means

Price switching from being delivered in one direction to being delivered in the other — visible on the aligned lower timeframe as **expansion met with expansion**: the move into the level was expansive, and the move away from it is immediately expansive too, with no drawn-out chop in between.

## The V-shape requirement

The change in delivery must come as a **V-shaped reversal**:

- Price purges the low (or high) — the stop run into the key level.
- Then sharply reverses, **closing above the body** of the down-move candle (bullish case) or **below the body** (bearish case).
- The shape is a V, not a saucer: expansion in, expansion out.

That closure above/below the body is the specific moment the swing becomes protected — on both the aligned timeframe *and* the higher timeframe whose swing it confirms.

## If there's no V-shape: wait

**Don't trade without the V-shape.** If price purges the level and then consolidates, drifts, or chops before eventually changing direction, that is not a valid confirmation — wait for a continuation setup instead ([[Order Block Continuation and the Stop Run Rule]]). In the [[NQ - 1043 SMT and Second-Stage Protected Highs|NQ example]], a purge followed by consolidation before the change was explicitly rejected as "not our V-shaped reversal" — the entry had to come from a later, cleaner sequence.

This is the same standard as [[Valid Reversal Signatures (The V-Shape)]] in [[Candle Profiling - Complete Framework]] — expansion met with expansion, strong close, no lackluster two-sided movement — applied here specifically to swing confirmation.

\# What Creates a Protected Swing

← [[Protected Highs]]

## The definition

A protected swing is a high or low that has earned the expectation of **not being revisited** while the current move plays out. That's what makes it tradable: you can position away from it (long above a protected low, short below a protected high) with a structural reason to believe it holds.

## The formation sequence (order block formation)

On the higher timeframe:

1. **A key level is hit or an SMT forms.** One of these two is mandatory — an old high/low taken, a fair value gap tapped, or a correlated-asset divergence. No key level and no SMT means nothing that follows can create protection.
2. **A reversal candle prints** on that higher timeframe.
3. **The aligned lower timeframe confirms** (per [[PDA Timeframes and Aligned Pairs]]) with a **change in delivery** and a **V-shaped reversal** — see [[Change in Delivery and the V-Shape Confirmation]].

Once all three are in, the low (or high) is protected **on both timeframes at once** — the lower-timeframe swing and the higher-timeframe swing it sits inside are both protected, and you can trade away from that candle onward.

## Both directions

- **Bullish**: key level/SMT below → reversal candle → aligned-TF V-shape closing *above the body* of the down move → **protected low** → trade higher.
- **Bearish**: swing high taken with key level/SMT above → reversal candle → aligned-TF V-shape closing *below the body* → **protected high** → trade lower.

## What this is in vault terms

This is the swing-level version of the same reversal anatomy used everywhere else: the key-level + SMT requirement mirrors [[The Two Non-Negotiables (Key Level and Open Draw)]] and [[SMT Confirmation Rule]], and the reversal candle is the [[What Creates a C2|C2 sweep]]. What this framework adds is the explicit **aligned-timeframe confirmation step** that stamps the swing as protected.

\# Internal Protected Swings for Continuation

← [[Protected Highs]]

## What they are

Once the higher-timeframe swing is confirmed protected (see [[What Creates a Protected Swing]]), you then look **inside** the move — at the internal price action on the aligned timeframe — for smaller protected swings that confirm continuation toward the draw on liquidity.

These internal swings are what let you stay with (or re-enter) the move after the initial entry: each one is a fresh, smaller protected high/low forming in the direction of the trade.

## How an internal protected swing forms

The bearish version (mirror for bullish):

1. The HTF protected high is already confirmed.
2. Price retraces up **into a gap** (a fair value gap on the aligned timeframe).
3. Price then **closes below the up-close candles** at that gap — order block behavior.
4. The high of that retracement is now an **internal protected high** — the candle has a protected high at the top *and* within it, and you can trade it lower toward the draw.

Each successful repetition creates the next one: tap a gap → close through the opposing candles → new internal protected swing → continuation. In the [[NQ - 6AM SMT Protected High|NQ example]] this chains repeatedly — "notice how you can just keep doing this."

## If price fails to close through the opposing candles

That's not a failure of the whole move — it triggers the stop-run sequence instead. See [[Order Block Continuation and the Stop Run Rule]].

## The hard boundary

All internal protection only lasts until the **draw on liquidity is met**. After that, these highs/lows stop being protected and become targets — see [[When Protection Expires (Draw on Liquidity Met)]].

\# Order Block Continuation and the Stop Run Rule

← [[Protected Highs]] · See also [[Internal Protected Swings for Continuation]]

## The confirmation an internal swing needs

Tapping into a gap alone is **not** enough to create a protected swing. The confirmation is the **order block continuation**: price taps the gap *and then closes through the opposing candles* (above the down-close candles for bullish, below the up-close candles for bearish). No closure through them → no protection yet.

## The stop run rule

When price taps the gap but **fails** to close through the opposing candles:

1. **Don't abandon the setup — wait for a stop run.** Price runs the nearby stops (purges a low/high).
2. After the stop run, look for the V-shaped reversal closing through the body ([[Change in Delivery and the V-Shape Confirmation]]).
3. If it delivers, **that** swing becomes the protected one — the earlier level that failed to confirm never gets the label.

And the rule loops: if the first stop run also fails to produce an order block, wait for the *next* stop run. In the [[ES - 30M to 3M Chain Confirming the 1H Swing|ES example]] this took two rounds — tap the gap, fail to close above the down-close candle, stop run #1, still no order block, stop run #2, order block forms → new protected low → rally to the highs.

## Why the failed level stays unprotected

The whole point of "protected" is that confirmed structure shouldn't be revisited. A level that couldn't close through its opposing candles never demonstrated that strength — so the market treating it as a stop-run target is expected behavior, not a betrayal of the framework.

\# When Protection Expires — Draw on Liquidity Met

← [[Protected Highs]] · See also [[Internal Protected Swings for Continuation]]

## The rule

Protected swings are only protected **while the draw on liquidity is still open**. The moment the draw is met:

1. The internal protected highs/lows **stop being protected** — they become targets, hunted for reversal plays.
2. **You stop looking for trades** in that direction. The move is done.

## The mistake this prevents

Price hits the draw, retraces back up toward your old protected highs, and it *looks* like the same short setup all over again. It isn't. Don't try to short it again — those highs are now liquidity for the *next* move, not structure for the old one. In the [[NQ - 6AM SMT Protected High|NQ example]]: once the draw was met, a high that got taken with a close below it just ran straight through — the down-close candles that would have been valid confirmations an hour earlier no longer meant anything.

## Why this fits the rest of the vault

This is the same "the trade is over at the draw" discipline that shows up everywhere else: [[Fixed 1-to-3 RR Discipline]] ends the trade at target rather than holding for home runs, and [[The Two Non-Negotiables (Key Level and Open Draw)]] says no open draw = no trade. Protection expiring at the draw is the structural version of the same idea — once the objective is met, the framework that justified the position no longer exists.

## Related

- [[The Two Non-Negotiables (Key Level and Open Draw)]]
